The following letter has been written by a group of mothers of students at Sharif University of Technology to one of our colleagues, and in fact to the entire body of colleagues at Sharif University of Technology. Its audience is, in reality, all professors and officials of Iranian universities.——————————————————————————————————————————————————————————————————-We are a group of mothers whose children have, in recent months, faced heavy disciplinary rulings and expulsion from university. What is most painful for us is that some of these students, in addition to the disciplinary case at the university and the expulsion ruling, have also faced punishment from the judicial system (mostly one to three years of imprisonment); that is, for a single offense at the university, they have faced two punishments from two institutions—the university and the judicial system! We ask you, if possible, to hear the voice of these mothers and, to the extent of your ability, help in reviewing the expulsion rulings, converting heavy punishments into more proportionate rulings, and providing the possibility for these students to return to the path of education. Sometimes a second chance can save a young person's life. We do not expect you to disregard the law; we only ask that alongside the law, fairness, proportionality of punishment, the circumstances of each student, and the future of a human being also be considered. If you have the means to follow up on these concerns or convey them to university officials or officials of the Ministry of Science, we sincerely request that you do not leave us alone. Source: @hesmashena

The real innovation of this plan lies in five points: The policy unit shifts from "carrier" to "service." Today, gasoline, gas, electricity, water, and transportation are largely managed in separate platforms. The plan says every decision should be measured based on the final output: "one unit of cooling," "one unit of heating," and "one unit of mobility" — with what combination of resources, technology, and cost they are provided. Four sources and three services are placed in a common decision matrix. For example, replacing gasoline with electricity is only desirable if its effect on the electricity balance, power plant gas, air, and network cost is measured simultaneously. This prevents "transferring imbalance from one carrier to another." Price reform becomes a functional contract rather than a financial measure. The price of excess consumption only rises when a real possibility of reducing consumption has been created; in mobility, that means travel options; in heating, controls and equipment; in cooling, low-consumption technology. This is an operational rule, not a slogan. Instead of buying equipment, the government buys "verified savings." Heaters, coolers, motors, buses, or boiler rooms are not the main subjects of payment. Payment is made against cubic meters of gas, kilowatt-hours of electricity, cubic meters of water, peak megawatts, or actually freed fuel. This change alters the financial and incentive model of the program. Three major consumption markets are redesigned simultaneously and complementarily. In mobility: vehicle–energy–time–cost; in heating: building–equipment–control–behavior; in cooling: electricity–water–peak–comfort. Thus, instead of dozens of scattered projects, three national "savings factories" are formed.

Education and health in the employment structure
In the European Union, the share of education and health in total employment is about 22 percent. In some Northern European countries, this ratio reaches 30 percent. More than 70 percent of jobs in these two sectors are held by women (approximately one-third of total female employment is in these two sectors).
In Turkey, Malaysia, Japan, South Korea, Algeria, and Tunisia, the share of these two sectors in total employment is about 11 percent, and in South America it averages between 11 and 12 percent.
The share of education and health in employment in Iran, Indonesia, Pakistan, and Bangladesh is about 8 percent. Apart from the role that education and health play in societal self-reliance, individual autonomy, citizenship, and social reproduction, even from an economic perspective, investment in these two sectors is highly effective in economic reproduction and growth. In Iran, input-output tables confirm this impact. Nevertheless, these two sectors in Iran face serious shortages in terms of financing, human resources, and infrastructure. This issue is particularly important given Iran's population dispersion and area. In this regard, this comparison might be interesting: the number of students in Iran is almost twice that of England, and the number of schools in Iran is more than four times. Iran's area is also about 12 times that of England. In Iran, more than 30 percent of students study in private and semi-private schools, while in England it is about 6 percent. However, the teaching staff of the two countries is almost equal.
In Iran, since the late 1980s, these two sectors have been the focus of government downsizing. Layers of the middle and upper classes also went along with these policies. But beyond the issue of government downsizing, the two institutions that are essential both for societal reproduction and economic growth were seen as surplus costs. According to one of the ministers of the first Hashemi government, some economists justified that these two sectors had the largest share of the government budget, and if only a little of these two were handed over to the private sector, the government's budget deficit would reach zero. He says we were "deceived" and accepted, but the more we handed over from these two sectors, the larger the budget deficit became.
Postscript: Education and health are two main areas of social investment, and there is great emphasis on investing in these two areas to face new risks. In successful experiences, due to the related and intertwined issues of these two areas, extensive job clusters have been formed at national and local levels.

entry.title: [jalaeipour] While the world faces an intensifying climate crisis, deepening inequality,…
entry.summary:
Source: @jalaeipour

While the world faces an intensifying climate crisis, deepening inequality, erosion of social trust, and extreme concentration of wealth, governments continue to seek to patch up markets, and economics has also viewed the "common good"—whether in the sense of public goods or common resources—only from the perspective of correcting market or government failures.
Mazzucato, professor at University College London and founder of the Institute for Innovation and Public Purpose, in her new book titled "The Common Good Economy: A New Compass" addresses the need to rethink the relationship between government, market, and citizens. In her view, the government should go beyond the role of repairing market failures and actively steer markets around the common good. She argues that a healthy economy is not built solely by relying on the market, but requires purposeful direction by public institutions. Instead of a minimal view of government, she speaks of a role in which the government coordinates businesses and society around shared missions—missions such as reducing inequality and combating climate change. You can see the book's table of contents and introduction here.
Postscript: Mazzucato's books "The Entrepreneurial State" and "The Value of Everything" have been translated into Persian.

🔘The way to tackle inequality
Angus Deaton, winner of the 2015 Nobel Prize in Economics, leads a team at the UK Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) focused on inequality. The fruit of this group's five years of study was published in April of this year; a book called "Challenging Inequalities," published by Princeton University Press, which has been widely welcomed. Martin Wolf says this book has five key conclusions about inequality:
1. Inequality of opportunity is inextricably linked to inequality of outcomes.
2. Redistribution of income and wealth matters, but so does the social status and dignity that comes from shaping one's own destiny.
3. The inequality-generating effects of policies related to trade, migration, and climate must be considered.
4. Seemingly fair market processes can have adverse consequences for inequality.
5. Economic growth still matters.

My surgeon friends there are truly exhausted by the number of operations on the wounded. This is not the way to run a country! Citizens in many areas where they need help, support, and refuge have been left to their own devices, and instead, in matters where they should be left alone, they are controlled. The continuation of this situation leaves no security for anyone. The police must be a civil, powerful, healthy, and respected force so that it can both play its natural role in any circumstances and be appreciated in proportion to its services. In other words, the police must be removed from the circle of political conflicts, because regardless of citizens' views toward their government, people with any inclination, when their lives and property are threatened by others, have no choice but to resort to the police. entry.summary:

Whisper 9. "The solution to the problem of life can be seen in the disappearance of this problem. Is this not the reason why those who, after a long period of doubt, have come to see the meaning of life, have been unable to say what this meaning is? Indeed, there are things that cannot be put into words. They show themselves. They are the mystical." The above passages belong to the groundbreaking work "Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus"; a time when Wittgenstein was fighting in the Austrian army and simultaneously working on the final version of the book, carrying it in his backpack. Undoubtedly, facing death on the front lines had a profound impact on the writing of the final passages of the "Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus," passages that carry strong existential undertones and are deeply intertwined with the being of the young Ludwig. There is no escape from addressing the "meaning of life," for man is a meaning-seeking and meaning-finding animal. A pure insight ripples through Wittgenstein's account of the meaning of life; a fluidity and elusiveness can be seen in it; one can neither ignore it, forget it, nor abandon it, nor can one formulate it neatly and do it justice in language, with the help of words, propositions, and phrases. As Rumi whispered to himself in the "Divan-e Shams": "Catch the hem of His grace, for He may suddenly flee / But do not pull Him like an arrow, for He may escape from the bow." Wittgenstein's tone and manner of phrasing in the above passages evoke the tone and phrases of the "Holy Bible." It is as if, as Jung and Kazantzakis have noted, the young Ludwig is the second creator of the world, seeking to complete the half-finished work of creation. In fact, he has given meaning to his life by producing original creative works and depositing an elixir within them; just as Forough and Sohrab did by creating the poems "Earthly Verses" and "Surah of Watching" in the collections "Another Birth" and "The Green Volume." 🔴The Effects of Believing Life Is Meaningless✍️Mostafa Malekian1️⃣ Boredom, Indifference, and a Vegetative LifeThe first effect of considering life meaningless is that life gradually takes on a vegetative state. A person no longer admires anything, has no deep interest in anything, and everything becomes monotonous and boring. Only when life is meaningful can a person praise something, become attached to something, and distinguish between different matters.In such a situation, life becomes the repetition of repetitions. Suppose someone is traveling from Tehran to Mashhad. Every time they stop at a gas station, they say: "I'm filling up the tank so I can reach Mashhad." This action has meaning because there is a destination.But if someone says: "I'm filling up the tank to reach the next gas station, and I'm going to the next gas station to fill up again and reach the next one," this cycle has no purpose and is mere repetition.Similarly, when life lacks meaning, a person's activities become aimless repetitions—just like a plant that bears fruit every year without knowing why.2️⃣ Nihilism, Anger, and FrustrationThe second consequence of considering life meaningless is nihilism. Nihilism means a person denies any meaning for life and even mocks those who attribute meaning to it.Moral psychologists believe such people typically suffer from:inner anger,a constant sense of frustration,and a kind of indifference toward the affairs of life.In their view, nothing truly matters; therefore, they don't feel much difference between various events and lose their sensitivity and attachment to life.3️⃣ Reduced Psychological Capacity to Cope with ProblemsThe third effect of considering life meaningless is the reduction of a person's psychological capacity. Meaning plays the same role for the mind and psyche that food plays for the body. Just as the body becomes weak if it doesn't receive food for several days, if life is meaningless for a person, their mind and psyche will also become weak and listless.As a result, a person finds less capacity to face life's problems and hardships. Enduring suffering means that after suffering befalls a person, they can tolerate and digest it within themselves. Coping with problems means having the strength to stand firm and resist before harm or injustice befalls them.According to moral psychologists, the meaningfulness of life strengthens both capacities in a person, but meaninglessness weakens both.@mostafamalekian
